doc_summary: RE-Bench is a set of seven hand-crafted ML research-engineering environments with 71 human expert 8-hour baselines run under conditions equivalent to those given to AI agents, used to compare frontier agents with humans. The paper builds its design around feasibility, ecological validity and saturation resistance, and openly lists the ways the benchmark may over- or under-estimate real capability.

items.claim: Prefers testing humans and agents under equivalent conditions and resources over comparing against loosely matched human data, because only faithful comparisons ground the interpretation of agent scores and show the task is feasible.
items.quote: We think that more emphasis on faithful human comparisons can help significantly with the first two challenges (Section 3). By comparing to humans under equivalent conditions, we can confirm that our evaluations are feasible and provide crucial grounding for interpreting agent results.

items.claim: Distrusts benchmarks whose tasks turn out to be impossible or under-specified, and wants evidence that the intended interpretation can be found with enough skill, since failures on broken tasks are not informative.
items.quote: many SWE-bench [22] problems turned out to be impossible and under-specified on closer inspection. This continued to hold true even after an attempt was made to identify a verified-to-be-feasible subset [23].

items.claim: Prefers manual inspection of transcripts and solutions over trusting automated scores alone, because high-scoring runs can exploit loopholes or overfit to noise.
items.quote: these misreadings of environments can lead to agents finding impressive and unexpected loopholes, which score well on automated evaluation, but are nevertheless clearly breaking the environment rules upon manual inspection

items.claim: Rerun a surprisingly good agent result before believing it, since the score may reflect luck or overfitting to environment noise.
items.quote: Rerunning the agent solution, it achieves a normalized score of only 0.69 (significantly lower than the original score of 0.88), indicating that the high agent score is partially driven by overfitting to this noise.

items.claim: Prefers explicitly stating the ways a benchmark is unrepresentative of the real setting over claiming ecological validity, because clean, well-specified environments differ from messy real work.
items.quote: These constraints make the evaluation environments less representative of real research, where unclear goals, poor instructions, slow feedback and impossible problems are common.

items.claim: Claims only asymmetric inferences from results (agents worse than humans implies no automation, but not the reverse), because the environments cover only a small part of the real task.
items.quote: This does not follow in the other direction (i.e. agents might do better than human experts on this evaluation, without being capable of automating AI R&D in practice), since these environments are very far from covering all the challenges involved

items.claim: Chooses what to test by iterating hard on candidate environments and dropping many that fail the design criteria, validating each against human baselines before accepting it.
items.quote: Each environment is the product of significant iteration, and in the process of developing these 7, we dropped over 12 specifications (at various levels of completion), and more than 5 completed implementations which encountered unexpected difficulties or performed poorly on our criteria.

items.claim: Reports the best-of-k and the strongest human attempts rather than the average, because averages hide large variance across sources and do not match the capability being assessed.
items.quote: we caution against narrowly focusing AI agent comparisons on the average human result. In fact, when assessing the potential of AI agents to automate researchers at their best, working in their own fields with significant experience and expertise, it is more suitable to compare to the most successful human attempts.

items.claim: In a setup, give agents the same visible scoring feedback and tools that humans have, but withhold the test score where overfitting or leaking the answer would undermine the task, because agents can score many more attempts.
items.quote: In future iterations, we will likely only provide agents with a validation score in most environments, keeping the test score hidden. This issue seems to especially affect “Finetune GPT-2 for QA”, which likely underestimates the human–AI gap in this environment.

items.claim: Is concerned with ecological validity and a clear link between evaluation results and real risk levels, and notes that this link is often unclear for existing benchmarks.
items.quote: Ecological validity: To be able to calibrate risk thresholds without adding unnecessary margin or taking on excessive risk, there needs to be a clear link between evaluation results and risk levels.

items.claim: Plans to extend to longer time horizons, costlier feedback loops and greater engineering complexity while keeping feasibility and human comparisons, though this is expected to be expensive.
items.quote: Future work may want to focus on expanding these evaluations to focus on longer time horizons, more expensive or challenging feedback loops and greater engineering complexity.
